title: Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies

blocks.text: Theme 3.1 · Investment, inclusion and sustainability · Focus area 15
Crowd in capital with targeted investment strategies

The province's capital pipeline funds airports, ports, roads, rail and the Metro waterfront, but almost none of it reaches regional product, bookability or community assets, where the growth case needs investment.

The growth case needs capital where the current pipeline does not reach. Visitors who travel beyond the Metro need beds, a booking route and finished product. The communities need assets a local seller can run. Yet committed capital closes the air gaps, not the regional ones (section 2.3). The province does not lack capital works. It lacks capital aimed at tourism outside the Metro.

Tourism funding is also tight, and below peer destinations (focus area 14). Fiscal pressure is prompting consideration of a tourism levy (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p25). The Department of Mobility sees a need for climate, development, blended-finance and private-sector models to fund tourism-enabling mobility (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p23). Its draft land transport framework goes further and plans its own business case for a tourist levy, to fund tourism transport (Western Cape Department of Mobility, draft Provincial Land Transport Framework, Apr 2025, ch12). Much of the product gap will therefore fall to private capital, which moves only where a case is ready.

The accommodation gap shows what is at stake. Province-wide, no mid-scale branded product sits between luxury estates and basic self-catering, and the Garden Route is short of quality-graded hotels for midweek, conference and business travel (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p94, p95). Mossel Bay reports that limited upper-upscale hotel capacity, particularly a recognised brand able to host conferences, holds back its higher-value and business demand (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p21).

blocks.message: Capital is committed to gateways and transport, and each district's tourism gaps carry no committed capital.

blocks.text: The evidence shows a gap in direction as much as in volume. The district tables list a large capital pipeline, and their gap columns show that none of it reaches regional product, SME bookability or township product. That finding is an inference from the tables rather than a printed statement, and no source gives a Western Cape tourism funding-gap figure [Western Cape tourism funding against the peer set: DEDAT and Wesgro budget data needed]. Kliptown is the warning case: capital built before an operator earned no operating income (section 2.1).

No scored list of tourism investment opportunities exists yet. The district gap-closure tables are its ready input: each names a gap, where it sits and whether any capital is committed to it. Scoring them for return, jobs and inclusion turns a list of needs into a ranked pipeline.

Wesgro should build the tourism investment pipeline the gap tables imply, and commit public capital only where demand has been shown. In 2027 and 2028 Wesgro's investment promotion team scores the gaps for return, jobs and inclusion and prepares the first investment cases (section 4.3). These cover mid-scale and conference-capable hotels in secondary nodes and accommodation at De Hoop and on Route 62. From 2029 it takes the cases to investors. DEDAT, the Department of Mobility and the City of Cape Town then test blended-finance vehicles and one levy case for the visitor economy. The pipeline is refreshed each year.

One rule runs across the portfolio: invest after demand, and attach a maintenance and marketing covenant to any public asset before it is let or upgraded (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p31, p15). The order matters. A levy or a blended-finance vehicle needs projects to fund, so both are tested only once the first cases exist. The levy also needs one case, not two. Separate tourism and transport levies would charge the same visitors twice. DEDAT should therefore agree with the Department of Mobility in 2027 that the Department's levy case covers destination management as well as tourist transport. That is this report's recommendation, not a position either department has taken.

blocks.text: A scored pipeline lowers the cost of finding a deal. Investors see ranked cases with demand evidence attached, rather than a list of district needs. Investing after demand reverses the Kliptown sequence, and covenants keep a public asset maintained and marketed after it opens. Wesgro has brokered community-linked capital before, though outside tourism. It brokered IDC funding for the Doringbaai abalone farm in 2015; the village trust holds 37% and the farm employs about 50 (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p25).

The comparators pair public direction with private capital. Chile funded about US$900 million of expansion at its gateway airport through a private concession awarded by its Ministry of Public Works (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p26). Melbourne paired its event strategy with 21% growth in hotel rooms, 5,000 new rooms and the entry of global hotel brands (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p18). The condition is demand first. Beds in secondary nodes pay only if the routes, events and booking work in Pillars 1 and 2 bring visitors to them.
